specPoints.text: be able to deduce the order (0, 1 or 2) with respect to a substance in a rate equation, using data from: i a concentration-time graph ii a rate-concentration graph iii an initial-rate method

primer.text: Graphs identify orders without any algebra. Concentration-time plots give a straight line for zero order, a constant-half-life curve for first order and an ever-steeper curve for second order; rate-concentration plots give a horizontal line, a straight line through the origin and a curve respectively. This note reads orders, half-lives and rate constants straight off the shapes.

lessons.title: Reading orders from concentration-time graphs
lessons.opening: A concentration-time graph announces its order by shape. Zero order draws a straight downhill line whose gradient is both the rate and k; first order draws a curve that flattens; second order draws a steeper curve. None of the algebra of rate equations is needed - the shape does the talking.
keyPoints: A zero-order concentration-time graph is a straight line sloping down, and its gradient equals the rate, which is also the rate constant k.
A first-order concentration-time graph is a downward curve that eventually plateaus as the reactant runs low.
A second-order concentration-time graph curves down more steeply than the first-order case.
For zero order the rate equation is simply rate = k, because concentration has no effect on rate.

low.restatement: Straight downhill line = zero order (gradient = rate = k); flattening curve = first; steeper curve = second.
low.analogy: Three drain shapes: a steady straight fall (zero), a fast start easing off (first), and a plunge that deepens (second).
low.examPointer: Do not confuse these with rate-concentration graphs - check which quantity sits on each axis first.

medium.restatement: The graph's slope is the rate at that instant; how that slope responds to the falling concentration is the order, drawn rather than computed.
medium.analogy: Braking in a car: constant pedal pressure (zero order), pressure easing as you slow (first), pressure building as you slow (second).
medium.examPointer: An exam favourite is quoting the gradient of a zero-order line as the value of k - say both words, rate and rate constant.

check.stem: The gradient of a zero-order concentration-time line gives

options.text: The rate of reaction, which is also the rate constant k
options.explanation: For zero order rate = k, so the constant slope carries both meanings.
The shape, not the gradient, announces the order.
Half-life is read from the axes, not this gradient.
Energy terms belong to Arrhenius work.

check.stem: A concentration-time graph that is a straight downward line indicates

options.explanation: The unchanging slope shows rate independent of concentration.
First order curves rather than running straight.
Second order is the steepest curve of the three.
Catalysis is not diagnosed by a straight line.

check.stem: The first-order concentration-time curve flattens at long times because

options.text: The reactant is being used up, so the rate falls with its concentration
options.explanation: Declining concentration slows the reaction, easing the slope.

options.text: The reaction has become zero order permanently
options.explanation: The order does not change during the run.

options.text: The products block the reaction completely
options.explanation: Blocking is not the mechanism here.

options.text: The temperature fell during the run
options.explanation: Temperature is held constant in these experiments.

check.stem: Compared with a first-order concentration-time curve, a second-order curve

options.text: Drops more steeply as time passes
options.explanation: Rate depends on the square of concentration, which falls faster.
A horizontal line belongs to a zero-order rate-concentration graph.
Plateau behaviour is the first-order signature at long times.
Reactant concentration only falls.

check.stem: For a zero-order reaction the rate equation is

options.text: rate = k, with no concentration term
options.explanation: Zero order removes the reactant from the expression entirely.
That is the first-order rate equation.
That is the second-order rate equation.
No inverse law appears in this treatment.

check.stem: State the shape of a zero-order concentration-time graph and what its gradient represents.
check.modelAnswer: A straight line sloping downwards whose gradient represents the constant rate, equal to k.

check.stem: State the shapes for first and second order on a concentration-time graph.
check.modelAnswer: First order: a downward curve that plateaus; second order: a steeper downward curve.

check.stem: Explain why the zero-order concentration-time graph has a constant gradient.
check.modelAnswer: The rate of a zero-order reaction does not depend on concentration, so as the reactant is consumed the rate refuses to change; an unchanging rate on a concentration-time plot is exactly an unchanging gradient, a straight line.

check.stem: A concentration-time graph starts steep and becomes steadily steeper. Which order does this suggest, and which rate equation accompanies it?
check.modelAnswer: The deepening steepness marks second order, and the accompanying rate equation is rate = k[A]^2.

lessons.title: Half-life behaviour and order
lessons.opening: The half-life is the time a concentration takes to halve, and its behaviour across successive halvings identifies the order: shrinking for zero order, constant for first, growing for second. One glance at a half-life table pins the rate law.
keyPoints: Under zero-order behaviour each successive half-life comes out shorter than the one before as the reaction runs.
A first-order reaction keeps one half-life throughout: every halving takes exactly as long as the last.
For a second-order reaction the successive half-lives increase as concentration falls.
Reading successive half-lives from a concentration-time curve is therefore a direct order test.

low.restatement: Half-lives that shrink mean zero order; steady half-lives mean first order; stretching half-lives mean second order.
low.analogy: Sharing a cake: a fixed slice time every round (first), quicker rounds as the cake shrinks (zero), slower rounds as leftovers dwindle (second).
low.examPointer: First order is the exam anchor: a constant half-life is the trademark proof you should quote.

medium.restatement: Half-life measures how long the current concentration needs to fall by half; since each order couples rate to concentration differently, each order slows or speeds the halvings in its own way.
medium.analogy: A leaky bucket: a constant drip time per halving (first), speeding drips as the bucket empties (zero), slowing drips as the level drops (second).
medium.examPointer: If given a table of halving times, decide increasing, decreasing or constant before naming the order.

check.stem: A reaction shows successive half-lives of 100 s, 50 s and 25 s. The order is

options.text: Zero order, whose half-lives decrease with time
options.explanation: Halving takes less and less time as the reaction progresses.

options.text: First order, whose half-lives are constant
options.explanation: First-order half-lives would all read 100 s.
Second-order half-lives grow, not shrink.
No fractional evidence appears here.

check.stem: The trademark of a first-order reaction is

options.text: A half-life that remains constant throughout the reaction
options.explanation: Each successive halving takes the same time.

options.text: A half-life that lengthens as the reaction runs
options.explanation: That is the second-order signature.

options.text: A half-life that shortens as the reaction runs
options.explanation: That is the zero-order signature.

options.text: A half-life that changes with volume
options.explanation: Half-life is a time, unaffected by vessel size.

check.stem: For a second-order reaction, as the reaction progresses the half-life

options.text: Increases, because the falling concentration slows the rate ever more
options.explanation: Rate tied to the square of a shrinking concentration makes halvings slower.
Decreasing half-lives mark zero order.
Constant half-lives mark first order.
No alternating pattern exists.

check.stem: The half-life method identifies order because

options.text: Each order couples rate to concentration differently, giving a characteristic pattern of successive halvings
options.explanation: The halving pattern is the order's fingerprint.

options.text: Half-life equals the rate constant for every order
options.explanation: Only under special relations is that true.
The whole method rests on order dependence.
Energy has no role here.

check.stem: A concentration-time curve shows the concentration halving every 40 seconds without exception. The rate equation is

options.explanation: A constant half-life is the first-order signature.
Zero order would show shrinking half-lives.
Second order would show stretching half-lives.
The half-life table already decides the order.

check.stem: State what happens to successive half-lives in a zero-order reaction.
check.modelAnswer: The successive half-lives decrease, taking less time for each halving as the reaction progresses.

check.stem: State the half-life pattern of a first-order reaction.
check.modelAnswer: The half-life remains constant throughout the reaction, each halving taking the same time.

check.stem: Explain why a constant half-life indicates first order.
check.modelAnswer: First-order rate tracks concentration, so each halving of the concentration halves the rate as well, and the time the next halving needs repeats identically - a signature unique to proportionality.

check.stem: A reactant's concentration falls from 2.0 to 1.0 mol dm^-3 in 30 s, then from 1.0 to 0.5 mol dm^-3 in 60 s. Deduce the order.
check.modelAnswer: The halving time stretched from 30 s to 60 s, so successive half-lives increase and the reaction is second order.

lessons.title: Reading orders from rate-concentration graphs
lessons.opening: Turned around, the same orders appear on rate-concentration axes. Zero order draws a horizontal line, first order a straight line through the origin, and second order an upward-sweeping curve. Paired with the concentration-time shapes, these graphs settle any order question twice over.
keyPoints: A zero-order rate-concentration graph is a horizontal line, since rate = k does not involve concentration.
A first-order rate-concentration graph is a straight line through the origin, since rate = k[A].
A second-order rate-concentration graph is an upward curve, since rate = k[A]^2.
Exam hints warn against mixing up concentration-time shapes with rate-concentration shapes.

low.restatement: Horizontal = zero; straight through the origin = first; upward curve = second - on rate against concentration axes.
low.analogy: Pay charts: a flat salary (zero), commission proportional to sales (first), and a bonus that grows with the square of sales (second).
low.examPointer: Check the axes before interpreting any line - the straight line that means first order here means zero order on the other pair of axes.

medium.restatement: Rate-concentration graphs read the rate equation directly: the vertical axis is the rate itself, so the shape traces the power of the concentration term.
medium.analogy: Pedal-to-speed maps in three cars: constant top speed (zero), linear pickup (first), quadratic surge (second).
medium.examPointer: When both graph types are offered, label each axis in your plan before writing an answer.

check.stem: A rate-concentration graph that is a horizontal line shows the reaction is

options.explanation: Rate stays flat as concentration changes.
First order is a straight rising line.
Second order is a rising curve.
Catalysis is not read from this shape.

check.stem: A straight line through the origin on a rate-concentration graph corresponds to the rate equation

options.explanation: Direct proportionality plots as a line through the origin.
That plots as a horizontal line.
That plots as an upward curve.
No inverse form appears here.

check.stem: The rate equation rate = k[A]^2 plots on rate-concentration axes as

options.explanation: The square relation bends the line upward.

options.text: A straight line through the origin
options.explanation: That is the first-order plot.
That is the zero-order plot.
Rate rises with concentration for positive orders.

check.stem: The classic exam confusion to avoid is mixing

options.explanation: A straight line means zero order on one graph and first order on the other.
Half-life is a separate test.
Orders never involve Ea.
Product concentrations rarely headline these graphs.

check.stem: On a rate-concentration graph, increasing [A] for a zero-order reaction leaves the plotted point

options.text: At the same height, because rate is unchanged
options.explanation: The horizontal line says rate ignores [A].
That is first-order behaviour.
That is second-order behaviour.
Rate never falls when a reactant is added here.

check.stem: State the rate-concentration shape for a first-order reaction.
check.modelAnswer: A straight line through the origin, reflecting rate = k[A].

check.stem: State the three rate-concentration shapes in order words.
check.modelAnswer: Zero order: horizontal line; first order: straight line through the origin; second order: upward curve.

check.stem: Explain why the first-order rate-concentration graph passes through the origin.
check.modelAnswer: With rate = k[A], setting the concentration to zero leaves a rate of zero, so the line must start at the origin and rise proportionally.

check.stem: A rate-concentration graph is a curve through the origin and the matching concentration-time graph shows increasing half-lives. Deduce the order and the rate equation.
check.modelAnswer: The curved rate plot and the stretching half-lives both point to second order, so the rate equation is rate = k[A]^2.

glossary.definition: The time taken for a reactant's concentration to fall to half its current value.
A plot whose shape reveals the order: straight line, flattening curve or steepening curve.
A plot whose shape traces the rate equation: horizontal line, straight line through the origin, or upward curve.
